This Section 3 does not apply to (a) internal use, research, or any commercial activity that is not Model as a Service, or (b) the Licensee's use of the Software as a component to power features of the Licensee's own product or service that is not a Model as a Service. They're allowing the use of this in commercial products, just not selling the model directly.

comments.author: sebmellen
comments.text: Nick is a force of nature. Highly recommend following him on X if you don't already. His launch post gives good context not found in the blog: > interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had > with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works https://x.com/nickcammarata/status/2110757819427574056?s=46

comments.author: bluejay2387
comments.text: The claims seem to be an overreach of what is actually proven. We've known about progressive feature complexity and the impacts of early training structures on later training for a really long time (since CNN's, The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, etc...) and neither of those phenomenon are mutually exclusive with parameter overloading. The Multimodal Gap work ( https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02053 ) seems to imply networks have a tendency towards condensed representations that are clearly not semantic and a bunch of other considerations are already on the table for discussion. I don't think these have all been considered sufficiently to start claiming we are around the corner from mechanistic interpretation.

comments.author: antics
comments.text: So we have here a massive evidentiary brief, the point of which is to argue that it is easier than we thought to, like, "sequence the AI genome" (in my estimation). We revisit famously-messy neurons, examine various tool failures, check places where messy things still hide, and catalog how "polysemanticity" is represented variously in the network. Once sequenced, the thinking goes, we'll be able to do things like: explain and anticipate failures; predict what happens when you modulate the pathway an input takes on its way to becoming output; reconstruct algorithms the models have learned. I'm not 100% sure this will work out like the mechinterp people think. If the neural representations and pathways are "clean" (organized into a a meaningful-to-humans hierarchy), it seems at least very plausible that the behaviors that AI xrisk people are worried about will mostly boil down to straightforward synthesis ( i.e. , mostly-linear-interpolation) of mostly-well-cataloged knowledge. And if that is true, then it does not seem hopeful that there would be a way to prevent the output they are worried about, other than just removing a bunch of the knowledge. So maybe there is no alignment solution at all.

comments.author: tomrod
comments.text: One of my greatest AI-related fears is that we build critical systems into kafkaesque hellscapes. Yes, nukes would be bad to give control to an AI with no workaround. But so are customer service groups of fraud departments at banks. A kafkaesque hellscape is where a customer or beneficiary of your service cannot get the help they need by policy and by design. Like getting Google on the phone, getting a non-scripted human 10 years ago in a call center, or now getting a non-agentic interaction on the phone. The scripts dominate the interaction. The IRS, for a time, would cut off your call if their wait system was too busy. That's a critical system in kafkaesque hellscape. Kudos to zlandes86, you have highlighted WHY these hellscapes start to pop up in systems where the human is removed. I am an AI user and builder -- I fully advocate for the human-augmented system, NOT the human-replaced system!

comments.author: zlandes86
comments.text: Hey, I'm Zach, the author of this. I had this idea as soon as Jev appeared: how would Jev and other decision models handle the Trolley Problem? So I ran Jev and 13 other models through many different versions of the question. I used resampling and multiple variations and orderings of each question so a random lucky phrasing wouldn't dominate the result. Happy to chat about the philosophical side of the article, strategies for prompting decision models, or anything on the methodology.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、Jevという意思決定モデルがトロッコ問題や危機的シナリオでどのように判断するか、その結果が人間を補助するシステムなのか、あるいは人間を完全に置き換える危険があるかという点。コミュニティでは、倫理的ジレンマへの対応とカフカ的官僚地獄の回避が焦点となった。

賛否: 一部は人間が最終判断を残す人間拡張システムを推奨し、AI単独の命にかかわる決定は官僚的手続きが救済を妨げると警告。他方では、JevはQwenやGemma等の既存構造化出力モデルと機能面で大きな違いがなく、マーケティングによる過大評価だと批判し、コスト・速度での優位性も疑問視した。

注目コメント: 作者Zachは複数のプロンプト変換と再サンプリングで結果のブレを最小化し信頼性を高めたと説明。別のコメントではアシモフの三法則を引用し、第一法則に従う限りは害を防げるが、実際のシナリオでは法則の衝突が判断を複雑にすると指摘し、倫理的制約の実装難易度を強調した。
stories.editor_note: Jevがトロリープロブレムに出会う は、倫理ジレンマをプログラミングの視点で論じた記事で、なぜ今話題かというと、日本の自動車メーカーが自動運転の倫理ガイドライン策定にAI倫理学者を積極的に採用している背景がある。実装時の意思決定ロジックが社会的に検証されるべきだという指摘が共感を呼んでいる。

comments.author: obviouslynotme
comments.text: I used to work on software that still uses Fortran from the 50's and is still in maintenance and use today. IIRC, it had ~700kloc of Fortran. It may be the oldest and largest Fortran codebase still in use. My first project there was removing all of the Hollerith from the code. Since Fortran predated strings, you had to manipulate them as integers. When you tied that to the original Fortran dynamic memory system, Dynosour, which used equivalenced arrays as pointers, it was a disaster. It also gave me an appreciation for JavaBeanFactoryFactory. The original Fortran limited identifiers to six characters, the first of which indicated whether the variable was an integer, logical (bool), or real (float). I will take a 100 character name over ILBNK1 every single time. GOTOs were surprisingly not a big problem, but structured code is definitely a bit easier to read, especially since it brought the practice of indentation with it. Overall, it was a great experience but I wouldn't want to do it again, even if the work was interesting.

comments.author: whartung
comments.text: FORTRAN was a very important language for me. Growing up on early micros, with BASIC, my father had Fortran for the TRS-80. I took a stab at learning it, but the documentation was reference for calling the compiler, not so much learning the language. And when I found a FORTRAN book, it was quite dated and talking about things like tapes and punches and what not. So, that effort stalled. But, my first quarter in college, I took a FORTRAN (77) class. FORTRAN taught on the schools CDC Cyber mainframe. This was quite a change from 8-bit PET BASIC. But, most importantly, it was exposure to much of the same concept that an 8-bit computer has, but from a different tact. This gave me more of a way to view things from a higher level, since I had to make them fit the two different views of how FORTRAN looked at things, how the Cyber presented things, and how BASIC and the PET were "same thing only different". It also gave me access to a multi-user system, and all of the interesting capabilities it offers. I remember when they put in their first lab of PCs, and how they started teaching folks Turbo Pascal on micro computers, and I just felt that the users were missing out on a bigger world. "Anyone" can access a PC or micro computer at home, but mainframe or multi user mini access, not so much. It's just a much bigger world out there, and we tend to baby duck what we first see. Different world today, never had to use FORTRAN professionally, but I am most grateful for the experience of learning it and its environment. Very powerful medium for broader learning. Also FORTRAN was the only notable computer thing I had "taught" to me (outside of my 20 minute introduction to BASIC by my high school teacher), pretty much everything else I self learned from books and such, even knowing the bulk of it before taking classes in school.

脆弱性を指摘する意見に対し、「当時はこういうバグが普通だった」とノスタルジー的に肯定する声と、現代のセキュリティ基準から見れば許容できないと批判する意見が分かれた。また、「Rewrite it in Rust」という提案に賛成する声（メモリ安全言語での再実装の必要性）と、レガシーシステムでは現実的ではないという反対意見がある。

comments.author: valdiorn
comments.text: I've been having a silent panic attack for the last 3 days, and I don't really have anyone to talk to that would understand my concern. I run a small pro audio company, we make guitar pedals and audio effects mostly. My current key objective is building up a processor similar to the Eventide H90, that would compete on having top-notch algorithms for reverb, delay, chorus etc. we already have single-effect pedals on the market that are very successful. In the past 72 hours I have ONE-SHOT decompiled 3 of my main competitors products, including the Strymon Big Sky. I just... have their award winning algorithms now. Like, I could in theory just stick them in a box and resell them. It took one prompt and 3 hours for opus 5.5 to work that out. The lexicon 224 then got added. While Claude was prepping It found someone else had already done the same thing 1 weeks earlier and dumped the result on GitHub, so it just stole that code and saved some time. It took all of 20 minutes to do the entire Ursa Major product range. And yes, I've tested them all - and they all sound phenomenal. I specifically asked Claude to first build an emulator and execute the original firmware/ROM so I could be certain it wasn't just making "something similar" but actually executing the same code. Then I asked it to convert it into a self contained c++ library and compare the result to the emulator. The problem is, everyone can now do this to my products as well. Basically, anyone with a Claude subscription can now rip of any best-in-class algorithm from any competitor. While I'm not going to do that, I know there are 30 Chinese companies that happily would. The moat of hardware effects processors has just vanished.

comments.author: revolvingthrow
comments.text: I reverse engineered almost all electronics I own. Does it have USB that does more than just charging? Connect it to a computer and let AI play with it. Unless it's heavily secured like a phone that's pretty much all you need to do. Making some old remote work with various devices? Simple. Dumping the entire state of Rodecaster and controlling it in any you want with software, or maybe a remote? Why not. Old printer no longer works with MacOS 27? Ask for new drivers and now it does. The printer 'debugging' was one of the funniest and most WTF situations I've been in lately. I used Claude for the drivers and was essentially used by it as a meat sock to diagnose what's happening. Was the text on each line progressively less visible, ie did grayscale work? How about quality between page 1 and 2, the first one should be lower DPI. Ok now unload the paper so I can see the error and add some handling for it. Good, now load paper again we'll check the duplex. If you are reasonably familiar with computers, it really is as simple as pointing a strong model at a device and burning some tokens. Feels like a fever dream, especially since I had very little idea about anything that has to do with hardware.

comments.author: synctext
comments.text: Interesting project, towards a decentralized Internet! The heavy lifting is done in this function, pairing. You link your personal devices together, solid idea [0]. This Flipflop project relies on the Iroh library for NAT/Firewall puncturing, external address discovery and overlay networking. Connecting two 5G devices, without a coordinating central server is possible, but very hard. Iroh simply relies on a server which you could self-host. Cool stuff, we stress tested it a while ago and it somewhat worked. NAT connectivity is unsolved. My university lab conducted one of the bigger puncturing studies a decade ago [1]. Recently, we also bought 40+ or something 4G and 5G SIM cards in Europe for puncturing [2]. My master student traveled Europe by bus to get these local SIM cards. He worked day-and-night to connect these weird symmetric 5G NAT filter boxes and got it working. Simple sync collision and birthday paradox brute force... It all works sometimes, but insufficiently reliable for mass-adoption. You can't build a decentralized social media ecosystem on top. Like Iroh, best to use a central server. So then you have legal liability for your users. Unless an AI agent buys the server fully autonomously using Bitcoin, next years students got that working[3] :-) [0] https://github.com/andunieee/flipflop/blob/62bb498520aacb60e... [1] UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild, https://inria.hal.science/hal-01597969v1/document [2] Mass Adoption of NATs: Survey and experiments on carrier-grade NATs, https://arxiv.org/html/2311.04658v2 [3] Self-replicating seedbox servers using programmable money, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05431

comments.author: cogman10
comments.text: I don't like it. I'm all for signing up for a contract if it can turn a runtime error into a compile time error. However, this looks like it just makes more runtime errors. At that point, these seem no better than `assert` except for the fact that they promise to really assert (probably). The article also points out a big problem which is "Importantly, this aspect of Contracts is why contract assertions must not be used for error handling and input validation: If a function has in-contract requirements to report certain events as errors, that handling must be done with standard C++ control statements that are not optional, never with contract assertions." That sort of muddy definition of what contracts are supposed to be used for is almost certainly going to make a mess. It's not input validation, but parameter validation.. but not really validation but rather checks which error out, but it's not errors we are producing.

comments.author: atleastoptimal
comments.text: I think beyond the specific elements of any domain AI eclipses humans in, overall, the notion of the thing that grants you status, prestige, and a living wage being commodified would spark in anyone a profound sense of dread. You are made one step closer to complete worthlessness, which will surely continue as AI becomes a more satisfying personal companion, a more worthwhile friend, lover, etc. How is one to feel safe in the progress of the future when the only hints of the wonderful post-scarcity utopia we can quantify so far is the removal of all human leverage via their labor? All it tells us is we will be bargaining with superintelligence with nothing to stand on, only a trust that the 5000 lab executives and researchers solved the most important research problem of all time on the first try.

For us, in the programming world, we will not have a 200 year grace period. AI could be used to help a large range of people, provide support, trusted advice. However because of the people who are funding it, that will not be the case. it will be used to reduce wages. comments.author: RGS1811
comments.text: This piece circles, without naming it, around the concept of “deontic scorekeeping” central to the work of Robert Brandom on semantics. The idea that our ability to create and sustain conceptual systems depends on the give and take of reasons within a social setting. Brandom has been front of mind for me lately because elements of his theory both explain why LLMs should work in principle, and where they are bound to be radically deficient. An LLM encodes the normative regularities of our linguistic/conceptual games into its weights, but it cannot be a real participant in our games because it is incapable of staking durable commitments or changing its dispositions over time. Worth reading: Robert Brandom, “Making It Explicit: Reasoning, Representing, and Discursive Commitment”

stories.summary_ja: 「AIが人間の専門性を置き換えることで、給与や社会的地位が商品化され、これまでの努力が意味を失うという不安が最大の論点だ。一方で、AIが真理探求を妨げ、検証されない主張が氾濫し、議論が音になるという懸念もある。歴史的に職業が消失した例（中世の織工）を挙げ、今回は猶予期間がなく、資金提供者が賃金削減のためにAIを使うと指摘する意見もある。哲学的には、Brandomの「deontic scorekeeping」を持ち出し、LLMは言語の規範を学べても、約束を変更できないため真の参加者にはなれないと指摘するコメントが注目された。また、数学者は発見の喜びが永遠に失われることを嘆いている。」
stories.editor_note: なぜ数学者が泣くのか知っている は、抽象的証明の美しさと困難さを詩的に語っているが、なぜ今話題かというと、日本では数学教育において「美しさ」を感じさせる指導法が注目されており、同様の感情共有が学習意欲向上につながるという見解が広まっているからだ。感情と理解の関係が教育現場で再評価されている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、HTTPヘッダーに仕込まれたプロンプトインジェクションがLLMエージェントに与える影響で、特に信頼できないヘッダーを盲目的に従うべきではないという懸念が中心だった。賛否は、一部の参加者が「ほとんどのインジェクションヘッダーはジョークや無害な試みであり、実際のリスクは低い」と主張する一方、Claude 4時代の拒否トリガー文字列を含むヘッダーは本物の脅威となりうるとして警戒すべきだと反論した点に分かれた。注目コメントでは、記事が冗長であることを指摘しつつ、「唯一真剣に取り組むべきはClaude 4の拒否トリガー文字列を含むヘッダーで、その他は単なるジョーク」と断じ、さらに「サーバーはエージェントを簡単に見分けて異なるコンテンツを返せるため、構造化メタデータではなくプレーンテキストに頼るLLMの仕組みそのものが問題」といった洞察が示された。 (398字)
stories.editor_note: HTTPヘッダーにおけるプロンプトインジェクション：2億1700万のウェブレスポンスが示すもの は、HTTPヘッダーに仕込まれたプロンプトがLLMに影響する現状を示したが、なぜ今注目かというと、日本ではWebアプリのセキュリティ診断ツールがヘッダーインジェクションへの対応を急いでおり、同様の大規模統計がリスク評価の基盤となっているからだ。防御策の標準化が求められている。
